Thought: Controlled benchmark: 100 OMIM phenotype entries rewritten by one model (Claude Opus 5.5) from exactly the cited papers, with only the generation strategy varied. The care is unusual: completion is treated as an outcome, there is an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis, a replicate-noise floor (1.0 pt), fixed fact lists that do not depend on the draft, matched ablations, a within-paper hidden-full-text experiment, a creation-date contamination check and planted-error tests, and the limitations are stated candidly. The headline findings are that the reading strategies are close (within ~2 pts) and that access to full text bounds coverage (77.4% vs 31.2%). The second is close to expected: the reference paragraphs were written from the full text. Everything rests on model judgements from the same family that wrote the drafts, and no human validated any of them. That is the main soundness gap at a top venue, because the primary endpoint itself is a model judgement of fact presence. One model and no second family means the 'strategy matters little' conclusion may be model-specific. The ML novelty is limited: the strategies are the authors' own re-implementations, and the benchmark is narrow (variant-centred ClinVar paragraphs, 93-entry comparison set). Strategies were developed on the evaluation entries. Clarity: careful but very dense, and the abstract packs in numbers. The header still says ICLR 2025 while the paper cites 2026 work. Fit for ICLR is acceptable as a datasets/benchmarks contribution, but the takeaway for the learning community is modest. Leaning reject but persuadable with human validation of the judge on a sample and a second model.
Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing curated genetics knowledge-base entries (OMIM phenotype entries) from exactly the papers the curators cited, with the causal gene withheld. One model writes every draft under shared guards (ontology lookup, HGNC normalisation, citation constraints), a claim-level audit against the cited papers, and shared scoring. Three paradigms are compared: read and write (direct long-context reading; an agentic curator), extract then write (evidence graph; case table), and memory first (recall then verify). The paper also tests a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand evidence from citing papers, reconciliation of case records, a learned curation guide). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists derived once from OMIM's curator-written allelic-variant paragraphs in ClinVar. Key results: on 93 entries that every strategy completed, the reading strategies lie within 47.2-49.1%, near a measured replicate-noise half-width of 1.0 point. Hiding full text in a within-paper experiment drops coverage from 77.4% to 31.2%. Differences between strategies grow with full-text availability, and a matched ablation suggests the extract-then-write deficit reflects extraction effort. The audit catches all 60 planted single-fact substitutions but checks fidelity to the source rather than correctness. Memory-only performance declines for newer entries, which serves as a contamination check.
Strengths: Strong experimental control: the model, sources, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed, so the generation strategy really is the only variable. This addresses a real comparability problem in prior work (FlyAOC, WikiCrow, GEN-KnowRD), each of which varies several factors at once.

Careful statistics: paired bootstrap intervals, sign counts, Holm correction for secondary measures, a measured replicate-noise floor (3 replicates on 30 entries) and judge-variation estimates. The paper interprets small differences against these noise floors rather than over-claiming.

Completion and safety-filter refusals are handled principled: strategies are compared only on entries every strategy completed, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 7). The paper also explicitly corrects an earlier analysis that biased the evidence-graph comparison.
Fixed fact lists split once, without sight of any draft, avoid denominators that adapt to each draft. The paper shows the earlier per-draft scoring inflated scores by 2-5 points.

The within-paper hidden-full-text experiment (Figure 2) and the missed-fact attribution (Figure 3) give causal and diagnostic evidence that access to the source, not the strategy, bounds agreement under current open access.
The matched ablation (Table 2) usefully separates implementation choices (extraction effort) from the intermediate representation itself, which tempers a naive 'extraction is worse' conclusion.

Unusually candid limitations and scoping, e.g. 'unsupported by cited papers is not wrong', the audit checks fidelity not correctness, and the planted-error test measures only sensitivity. A per-entry release of drafts, verdicts and scores is promised, and the cost accounting is transparent.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. The primary endpoint (fact present / partly / absent / contradicted), the audit verdicts, the missed-fact attribution and the contradiction adjudication are all model judgements by the same family that wrote the drafts. Without even a small curator-annotated sample (e.g. 200-500 fact judgements) giving agreement rates, the absolute numbers and possibly the strategy ordering are not validated. Self-preference effects (Panickssery et al.) are cited but not measured.

Single model. The central conclusion, that reading strategies are close, may be specific to a strong long-context model on short inputs (2-12 references). With no second model family (including a weaker or shorter-context one), the generality that would interest the ICLR audience is untested.

The headline access result is largely expected. The reference paragraphs were written by curators who read the full papers, so drafts written from abstracts would naturally cover fewer of those facts. The experiment quantifies this well, but its scientific surprise is limited. The comparison is also asymmetric: only the full-text draft went through the repair round.

The reference is narrow and indirect: variant-centred OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar, plus HPO annotations (partly derived from OMIM). The narrative phenotype sections, which are what curators actually write in a phenotype entry, are not compared. Drafts make about twice as many statements as the reference has facts, so precision with respect to the curated content is essentially unmeasured beyond the audit.

Strategies were developed on the same entries they are evaluated on, with no held-out development set. Combined with the small effect sizes being interpreted, this is a concern for the strategy comparison, even if it matters less for the access result.

Limited methodological novelty for ICLR. The strategies are the authors' own re-implementations of known paradigms, and the add-ons are small-scale (e.g. two reflection rounds on 27 entries for the learned guide), so the null results are weak evidence. The contribution is mainly the benchmark and the careful protocol in a narrow biomedical domain.

The planted-error test (60/60 flagged) has no unaltered controls, so the false-positive rate is unknown and the claim about audit sensitivity is half-measured. Omissions and misattributions are untested.

Presentation: the text is very dense and number-heavy, especially the abstract and Section 4, which makes the main message hard to extract on first read. The header reads 'ICLR 2025' while the paper cites 2026 work and names a 2026 model.
Questions: Can you provide human (curator or trained annotator) validation of a random sample of fact-presence judgements and audit verdicts, reporting agreement with the model judge per category (present / partly / absent / contradicted)? Would the strategy ordering survive the observed disagreement rate?
Have you run any strategy with a second model family, even on a subset (e.g. the 30 replicate entries)? Does the closeness of the reading strategies hold for a weaker or shorter-context model?
In the hidden-full-text experiment, how large is the full-text vs abstract gap if the full-text draft is taken before the repair round, so that the conditions are symmetric?

How were strategy prompts and design choices tuned, and on which entries? Could you evaluate on a fresh held-out sample (e.g. the 2026 entries, for all strategies) to rule out overfitting to the development entries?
What is the false-flag rate of the audit on unaltered paragraphs, and how does it detect omissions or misattributed citations?
Since HPO annotations are partly taken from OMIM (476 of 2,311), are the synopsis results different when restricted to the HPO team's own curation?

For the claim that strategy differences grow with full-text availability: can the matched ablation entries (which are weighted towards full text) be used to make this a within-entry rather than across-entry comparison?
Limitations: One model family wrote, audited and judged everything, with no human validation (acknowledged).
Small evaluation set (93 compared entries; 46 in the access experiment; 38 in the ablation), with short reference lists only. Large entries are exploratory.
Only open-access text without supplementary material, where much variant-level data resides (acknowledged).
Strategies were developed on the evaluation entries (acknowledged).
The reference covers variant-centred paragraphs, not the phenotype narrative sections curators write.
Safety-filter refusals remove entries unevenly, and their reasons are not visible.
Contamination can be checked only through creation-date trends, since the model's training cut-off is unknown (acknowledged).
